{
  "oa": 2,
  "strengths": [
    "The paper clearly explains why deterministic prediction from pixels does not eliminate confounding when explanations concern a subset of interpretable concepts. This distinction offers useful insight for explainability and causal-discovery researchers.",
    "Using PAGs and FCI is principled under the stated assumptions. The background knowledge that model predictions cannot cause preexisting image features is defensible, and the representation explicitly accommodates unresolved causal directions.",
    "The synthetic example makes omitted-feature confounding concrete. The real-data applications, bootstrap analyses, and alternative discovery algorithm help illustrate the workflow. The discussion thoughtfully acknowledges limitations involving faithfulness, annotation errors, feature selection, and identifiability."
  ],
  "weaknesses": [
    "Necessary: The empirical interpretations exceed what the reported statistic establishes. Section 6.3 pools directed and partially directed edges, although a partially directed edge remains compatible with pure confounding. Moreover, absence of adjacency to the prediction does not exclude an indirect causal pathway. Consequently, statements in Section 6.4 that particular features are important determinants while others are not are insufficiently supported. Report definite versus possible causal status separately, consider ancestry through intervening variables, and narrow the substantive conclusions accordingly.",
    "Necessary: The X-ray sampling scheme requires a selection-bias analysis. Section 6.1 selects pneumonia cases and controls specifically having 'no findings,' so inclusion depends on both diagnosis and the explanatory findings. This can induce dependencies that latent-confounder handling alone does not resolve, contrary to Section 3's dismissal of selection bias as irrelevant. Justify the causal interpretation under this sampling scheme, use an appropriate analysis, or present this application as exploratory.",
    "Necessary: The reliability of the conditional-independence decisions is insufficiently established. The X-ray cohort contains only 240 images, while the bird analysis uses multivalued variables and conditioning sets containing up to four variables. Sparse contingency tables could compromise the chi-square tests; bootstrap repetition does not correct such miscalibration. Report effective discovery sample sizes and sparse-table handling or provide suitable calibration evidence. The substantial changes between FCI and GRaSP-FCI, particularly for wing shape and crown color, also require more restrained claims about the identified bird features.",
    "Necessary: Example 1 and Appendix A do not establish the claimed Shapley counterexample as written. Appendix A.2 leaves the supposedly unmeasured Z3 fixed inside coalition values, including the baseline, rather than defining an adjustment estimator using the observed variables. Appendix A.1 also retains the marginal distribution of Z1 when setting its causal parents Z2 or Z3, requiring clarification of whether these are input-replacement values or interventions in the stated SCM. Define a consistent estimand and observed-data estimator, then repair or remove the derivation.",
    "Optional: Repeated synthetic experiments with known intervention outcomes would help quantify practical reliability. Comparisons using the same concept annotations would also better isolate the benefit of causal discovery: the current LIME/SHAP illustrations primarily demonstrate differences in explanatory units and local versus population-level targets."
  ]
}

strengths: The paper clearly explains why deterministic prediction from pixels does not eliminate confounding when explanations concern a subset of interpretable concepts. This distinction offers useful insight for explainability and causal-discovery researchers.

Using PAGs and FCI is principled under the stated assumptions. The background knowledge that model predictions cannot cause preexisting image features is defensible, and the representation explicitly accommodates unresolved causal directions.

The synthetic example makes omitted-feature confounding concrete. The real-data applications, bootstrap analyses, and alternative discovery algorithm help illustrate the workflow. The discussion thoughtfully acknowledges limitations involving faithfulness, annotation errors, feature selection, and identifiability.
weaknesses: Necessary: The empirical interpretations exceed what the reported statistic establishes. Section 6.3 pools directed and partially directed edges, although a partially directed edge remains compatible with pure confounding. Moreover, absence of adjacency to the prediction does not exclude an indirect causal pathway. Consequently, statements in Section 6.4 that particular features are important determinants while others are not are insufficiently supported. Report definite versus possible causal status separately, consider ancestry through intervening variables, and narrow the substantive conclusions accordingly.

Necessary: The X-ray sampling scheme requires a selection-bias analysis. Section 6.1 selects pneumonia cases and controls specifically having 'no findings,' so inclusion depends on both diagnosis and the explanatory findings. This can induce dependencies that latent-confounder handling alone does not resolve, contrary to Section 3's dismissal of selection bias as irrelevant. Justify the causal interpretation under this sampling scheme, use an appropriate analysis, or present this application as exploratory.

Necessary: The reliability of the conditional-independence decisions is insufficiently established. The X-ray cohort contains only 240 images, while the bird analysis uses multivalued variables and conditioning sets containing up to four variables. Sparse contingency tables could compromise the chi-square tests; bootstrap repetition does not correct such miscalibration. Report effective discovery sample sizes and sparse-table handling or provide suitable calibration evidence. The substantial changes between FCI and GRaSP-FCI, particularly for wing shape and crown color, also require more restrained claims about the identified bird features.

Necessary: Example 1 and Appendix A do not establish the claimed Shapley counterexample as written. Appendix A.2 leaves the supposedly unmeasured Z3 fixed inside coalition values, including the baseline, rather than defining an adjustment estimator using the observed variables. Appendix A.1 also retains the marginal distribution of Z1 when setting its causal parents Z2 or Z3, requiring clarification of whether these are input-replacement values or interventions in the stated SCM. Define a consistent estimand and observed-data estimator, then repair or remove the derivation.

Optional: Repeated synthetic experiments with known intervention outcomes would help quantify practical reliability. Comparisons using the same concept annotations would also better isolate the benefit of causal discovery: the current LIME/SHAP illustrations primarily demonstrate differences in explanatory units and local versus population-level targets.
